verses.1:
Al-Mizan explains that nafal means an excess, so anfāl denotes both ownerless acquisitions—such as ruins, land without an owner, and property without an heir—and spoils of war, because booty and captives exceed a battle’s primary aim of defeating the enemy. Dhāt, though originally meaning a possessor of something, came into usage for a thing’s essence; dhāta baynikum therefore denotes the bad relationship between two parties. To rectify it means ending their estrangement and bad blood.

Exegetes have disagreed over the verse’s reading, whether anfāl means booty generally, the booty of Badr specifically, or fayʾ, and whether the ruling was abrogated by the khums verse. Reports from the Prophet’s family, Ibn Masʿūd, Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, and Ṭalḥah ibn Maṣraf recite yasʾalūnaka al-anfāl, “they ask you for the spoils,” rather than the common yasʾalūnaka ʿan al-anfāl, “they ask you about the spoils.” The commentary prefers the common reading: saʾala ʿan means seeking knowledge of a ruling or information, whereas saʾala with a direct object means asking for something. The command, “Mind Allah and rectify what is between yourselves,” shows that two parties were disputing over booty and sought the Prophet’s judgment to settle the dispute.

Although anfāl has a wider sense, it here concerns spoils taken in fighting against the enemies of the faith, not booty from Badr as such. Yet the ruling extends to every kind of anfāl: ghanīmah and fayʾ alike belong to Allah and the Messenger, and the believers possess no immediate share in them. God ends the quarrel by removing the property from the contestants’ hands and placing its authority with Himself and His Messenger. Their dispute suggests that they had understood some prior, general or ambiguous permission to claim booty in ways favorable to themselves.

Reading the verses on booty together, Al-Mizan holds that the sūrah concerns Badr and its aftermath. Verses (8:67-69), which censure those who urged ransom for captives and then permit use of what was acquired in war, apparently led some to suppose that they owned the spoils. They consequently disputed whether all those present or only fighters were entitled, whether shares differed, and whether horsemen exceeded foot-soldiers. Verse (8:1) corrected this assumption: permission to “eat” what was acquired means using what the Prophet distributes, not owning it. After the dispute ceased, the Prophet divided the booty equally, including shares for some who had neither attended nor fought, without distinguishing horsemen from foot-soldiers. Verse (8:41) was then revealed later, as its reference to the day when the two hosts met indicates; the Prophet took a fifth from what had been allotted, leaving the rest to them.

Thus neither (8:1) nor (8:41) abrogates (8:69), and (8:41) does not abrogate (8:1). The three passages together establish that Allah and His Messenger own the spoils; four-fifths may be distributed to the fighters for their use, while a fifth, the khums, belongs specifically to Allah, the Messenger, the near of kin, and others. Since ghanāʾim are called anfāl as excess acquisitions, the ruling is general. The first al- in al-anfāl could possibly indicate the particular booty under dispute, while the second denotes the whole class or all its instances, explaining the noun’s repetition. Accordingly, “the anfāl are for Allah and His Messenger” is an overarching rule covering ownerless properties and acquisitions, including ruins, mountain tops, canyon-clefts, kings’ wealth, and wealth without an heir. Booty in the specific sense concerns Muslim soldiers under the Prophet’s command; the remaining anfāl are under Allah’s and His Messenger’s ownership.
verses.2:
Al-Mizan presents verses (8:2-4) as an elaboration of the command to fear Allah, reconcile, and obey Allah and His Messenger if one is a believer. The verses select five qualities that bring the other qualities of faith with them: hearts tremble at Allah’s remembrance; faith increases when His signs are recited; believers trust in their Lord; they establish prayer; and they spend from what Allah has given them. The first three belong to the heart and the latter two to outward action.

These qualities follow the natural growth of faith. Its first light produces reverence and fear at Allah’s mention. As reflection upon the divine signs deepens understanding, faith increases until it becomes certainty. This increase is one of quality, intensity, and perfection, not an increase in believers’ number. When faith reaches maturity, one recognizes that all affairs return to Allah, and therefore relies upon Him, follows His will and ordinances, and accepts what He has allotted. Faith then impels worship through prayer, the servant’s humble relation to his Lord, and service to society through spending on those in need from whatever sustenance one has received, whether wealth, knowledge, or something else.

Those who possess these traits are truly believers and receive ranks before their Lord, forgiveness, and an honorable sustenance. Forgiveness is pardon for sins, and honorable sustenance is the blessings of the Garden. The ranks are degrees of nearness, station, and spiritual honor; such nearness entails forgiveness and the Garden. They do not mean that every believer possesses every rank, for faith itself has degrees among believers. The commentary therefore rejects the view that darajāt simply means levels of Paradise, although greater nearness to Allah corresponds to higher levels there.

Al-Mizan connects verses (8:5-6) to the ruling that spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger: God’s decree was right even though some disliked it, just as His sending them forth from their homes was right although a group of believers disliked and disputed it after its truth had become clear. Both matters served their religious and worldly welfare, though they did not perceive this. The alternative connections of the passage either to their disputing alone or merely to the word “truth” are considered remote from the context.

Here ḥaqq is the opposite of falsehood: an established act with desirable real consequences, so that Allah’s sending them forth was something that had to be done. It does not mean revelation or jihad. Yujādilūnaka fī al-ḥaqq means that they quarrelled with the Prophet about this truth. Their aversion and argument after its clarity resembled people being driven toward death while seeing the instruments of execution before them.

verses.7:
Al-Mizan explains that the promise of victory over one of the two companies at Badr displays God’s favor, so that the believers should recognize that His commands and decrees are right, serve their interests, and bring their efforts to fruition. They should therefore leave their affairs to Him, obey the Messenger, and not resent His choice. The two companies were the Quraysh caravan, the ʿĪr, carrying their goods and wealth with forty men including Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb, and the Nafīr, their army of about one thousand. The believers hoped for the caravan, which had fewer men and less armament; ghayra dhāt al-shawkah denotes this company, while shawkah, derived from “thorns” or “spikes,” figuratively denotes force or vehemence.

God instead willed that they meet the Nafīr, though the Muslims were weak before its strength, valor, and numbers. To verify the truth means to demonstrate and establish it through its effects, by God’s decree to aid His prophets and give ascendancy to His true religion. Although kalimātihi may be read as “His words,” the reading kalimatihi, “His word,” seems better. To “sever the root” of the unbelievers is figurative language for eradication that leaves no trace and permits no return. Thus God promised victory over either company but chose victory over the army in order to manifest His decree and root out the faithless.

In verse 8, li-yuḥaqqiq indicates the final end and refers back to God’s promise: He does not fail in His promise to show the truth of truth and the falsity of falsehood, however much the guilty hate this. This purpose is not merely a repetition of the preceding statement that God willed to verify the truth through His words.

Tastaghīthūn in verse 9 means seeking aid, support, and victory, and mumiddukum means assistance. Murdafin means “following.” Read alongside the angelic aid mentioned in Sūrah Āl-i ʿImrān, the thousand angels in this verse were sent following the three thousand angels. The commentary consequently rejects interpretations that make them two successive contingents of one thousand, make some angels follow others, make the angels follow the Muslims as riders behind them, or make the Muslims follow angels who had gone before the army.

The pronouns in verse 10 refer to God’s aid through the angels. He sent them to bring glad tidings and tranquility to the believers, not to destroy or kill the faithless by their own hands. The angels increased the apparent mass of the Muslims among whom they were intermingled, reassured them, and cast terror into the idolaters. This supports the view that they did not fight: ʿAlī killed half or a third of those slain, and the other Muslims killed the rest. Victory truly belongs to God alone, not to superior numbers, strength, or courage; at Badr the idolaters possessed these advantages, whereas the Muslims were few. God’s might and wisdom underlie both His aid and its manner.

Nuʿās, in verse 11, is the first, light stage of sleep, and amnatan means security; “from Him” means from God, though some exegetes take it as from the enemy. The sleep that came upon the believers was God-given security, since a fearful person neither becomes drowsy nor sleeps. The rain purified them, removed Satan’s rijz—his deceptive whispers, anxiety, and seduction—and strengthened their hearts, that is, made them brave. It also gave them firm footing, either by making the sand sticky or by making their hearts steadfast. The verse supports a narrated account in which the enemy had first occupied the water source, while the believers suffered thirst, ritual impurity, and unstable sand; Satan exploited this to agitate them, but God sent rain to cleanse them, remove their major and minor impurities, firm their ground, and make the enemy’s ground muddy.

Verse 12, like the preceding verses, is an adverbial clause recalling the time of these events. “Strike above their necks” apparently means strike their heads, while “their every fingertip” means their hands, feet, or fingers, preventing them from wielding weapons. Apparently, the command may be addressed to the angels. It may be literal, or figurative for humiliating and terrifying the enemy until they cannot retain their weapons. It is also possible that it addresses the believers, emboldening them, strengthening their hearts and feet, and inciting them against the idolaters.

Shāqū means to oppose, violate, or infringe, and derives from a root meaning division: one who breaks away inclines to one side against the other. The punishment inflicted on the idolaters follows from their persistent opposition to God and His Messenger, and whoever secedes from them faces a mighty requital. Finally, “Taste this” is an emphatic address to the faithless: disgrace has overtaken them for them to taste, and punishment in the Fire awaits them beyond it.

Thus, this verification of truth, though similar in sense to the preceding mention of God’s will to verify it through His words, is not merely a repetition.

verses.15:
Al-Mizan explains that laqītum denotes a mutual, close encounter: each side comes face-to-face with the other. It may also denote sensory or inward perception, while “meeting with God” signifies the Resurrection. Unlike ijtimāʿ, liqāʾ specifically implies meeting at close range.

Zaḥfan signifies an army’s gradual but determined advance to fight, or a contingent swarming upon an enemy. Tuwallūhum al-adbār means turning one’s back to the enemy in flight and defeat. The command therefore forbids believers to flee when they encounter the rejectors advancing for battle.

The commentary holds that the injunction is general, not confined to particular persons, circumstances, or the Battle of Badr. The claim that it applied only at Badr has no basis, especially because the context indicates that these verses were revealed after Badr and conclude the passage that begins with the ruling on spoils.
verses.16:
Al-Mizan explains that mutaḥarrifan denotes a combatant who angles or veers away amid battle as part of a stratagem, such as an ambush. Mutaḥayyizan ilā fiʾah means withdrawing to join a company rather than facing the enemy alone. Bāʾa, literally returning and remaining in a place, here means returning accompanied by God’s wrath.

Together with the preceding verse, the passage prohibits fleeing whenever believers meet or are approached by the rejectors for battle. Whoever flees incurs divine wrath and has Hell as his destination, except one who withdraws for a military stratagem or to join another contingent; such withdrawal is not blameworthy.
verses.17:
Al-Mizan holds that the verse unquestionably concerns Badr: the Prophet cast a handful of gravel at the enemy, and the believers swiftly prevailed. By declaring that the believers did not slay and the Prophet did not throw, while attributing both acts to God, the verse reminds them that God—not they or the Prophet independently—was the true actor in this blessing.

The victory could not be explained by ordinary causes alone: the believers were a small, poorly equipped force against a much larger and better armed enemy. God sent angels to strengthen the believers and terrify the polytheists, and brought defeat upon the enemy through the Prophet’s handful of gravel. The believers truly fought, killed, captured, and routed their opponents, and the Prophet truly threw the gravel; nevertheless, these natural and human causes do not conflict with God’s higher causation, care, and oversight.

“So that He could try the faithful, a beautiful trial from Himself” explains the divine purpose of these acts. The pronoun in minhu apparently refers to God: He acted for a good known to Him, testing the believers beneficently and granting such blessings as the defeat of their enemies, the elevation of monotheism, and relief through spoils. “Allah is hearing, knowing” further explains that He gave this beautiful trial because He heard their pleas and knew their condition.

The initial fa- links the verse to the preceding enumeration of divine aid beginning with [Remember] when you sought aid from your Lord (8:9): the angels, drowsiness, rain, steadfastness, and terror cast into the enemy are summed up by the statement that God slew and threw. On this reading, verses 8:15-16 are a stylistic interpolation, with the present verse returning to “…Then strike above their necks and their every fingertip” (8:12), or else it connects to the equivalent overall sense of the preceding statements. Al-Mizan regards this as correct, rather than the suggestions that the verse merely follows a command to fight in order to remind them of divine aid, reproves boasts such as “I killed so-and-so,” or uses fa- only as a non-causal connective.
verses.18: Al-Mizan, following Majmaʿ al-Bayān, takes dhālikum wa anna Allāh as meaning: the matter is as stated, and God is the one who weakens the rejectors’ schemes. Dhālikum and anna Allāh are both nominative; dhālikum is not a subject whose predicate begins with fa-, since such a construction is grammatically invalid. The verse thus confirms the preceding account of divine action by declaring that God frustrates the rejectors’ plots.
verses.19:
Al-Mizan holds that the verse, with its repeated pattern—“if you demand,” “if you desist,” and “if you return”—is addressed wholly and sarcastically to the faithless, not to the believers. If the idolaters sought God’s judgment and victory against the believers, that victory had already come at Badr, where the truth was manifested and the believers prevailed.

They are therefore told to cease plotting against God and His Messenger. If they return to their hostility, God will return to weakening their schemes, and their numbers will avail them nothing, as they did not at Badr. God is with the faithful, who therefore cannot be vanquished.

This reading accords with reports that at Badr Abū Jahl prayed for victory over Muḥammad, or, in a report from Abū Ḥamzah preserved in sources such as Majmaʿ al-Bayān, prayed that victory be given to the followers of whichever of the old and new religions pleased God more. The commentary rejects the attempt of some exegetes to address the verse to the faithful.
verses.20: Al-Mizan explains that “from him” refers to the Prophet. Believers are commanded not to turn away while hearing him convey the true call and the commands and prohibitions that reform their worldly and otherworldly lives. Though expressed generally, the exhortation concerns the rules of war.
verses.21:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse reproves polytheists who claimed to hear the truth but did not truly listen. The first “hear” in samiʿnā means merely that the sound of the truthful speaker reached their ears; the second, in lā yasmaʿūn, means listening receptively and yielding to what is heard. Had they truly listened, they would have responded positively.

Although framed as an address to the idolaters, the verse remains part of the exhortation to believers: faith and the call to truth will overcome faithlessness and falsehood, so believers must obey God and the Messenger and not turn away after hearing the truth, lest they resemble those who professed hearing without it.

The commentary considers it possible that the verse refers specifically to Meccans who had accepted the Prophet inwardly but, being confined by their fathers, marched with Quraysh at Badr. A narration names Qays ibn al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah, ʿAlī ibn Umayyah ibn Khalaf, al-ʿĀṣ ibn Munabbih ibn al-Ḥajāj, al-Ḥārith ibn Zamʿah, and Qays ibn al-Fākah ibn al-Mughīrah; on seeing the Muslims’ small number, they said that their religion had deceived them and suffered the fate of the idolaters. The suggestion that the verse refers to the Jews of Banū Qurayẓah and al-Naḍīr is unlikely.
verses.22:
Al-Mizan takes the verses to condemn the faithless rejectors already under discussion. The definite article in al-ṣumm al-bukm refers back to them: they are the vilest creatures because they are deaf and dumb toward truth, unable to receive it into their minds or confess it.

Their deafness and muteness mean that God has deprived them of hearing and accepting the word of truth because He found no khayr in them. Khayr here is an inward disposition prepared to receive and acknowledge truth. Had God found such receptivity, He would have enabled them to hear; but even if He made them hear while that inner goodness remained absent, they would turn away in rejection. Thus there is no objection that hearing would itself have produced goodness, for the conditional statement presupposes its absence.

verses.24:
Al-Mizan explains that the Messenger’s call is the divine call that gives human beings true life, rescues them from destruction, and requires a firm response in view of God’s nearness and the final gathering before Him. This life is not mere bodily life, sensation, or free choice. It is the spiritually true and happy life, realized through beneficial knowledge and righteous deeds and completed in the higher life of the hereafter, whereas worldly life is shared with beasts and may be absorbed in delusion.

Human beings possess an innate fiṭrah that recognizes true beliefs and deeds, distinguishes benefit from harm, and directs them toward the happiness proper to their existence. Since this guidance is embedded in creation, it does not itself err. Deviation arises instead when intellect becomes heedless of this guidance and follows desire, conjecture, and the embellishments of the devils (shayāṭīn). Departing from fiṭrah forfeits the knowledge and righteous action necessary for happy life and leads to ignorance, corrupt choice, and the condition of the dead.

The call “to that which gives you life” is therefore the comprehensive call of Islam, understood as conformity to fiṭrah in beneficial knowledge and righteous deeds. It is not restricted to jihad, martyrdom, faith alone, truth, the Qur’an and religious knowledge, or Paradise, though each may be an application of the verse. It may encompass the entire Prophetic call, elements of that call that enliven hearts, or its final result: truly happy life in God’s presence.

Al-Mizan interprets yaḥūl as “intervenes” or “stands between,” and qalb in its usual Qur’anic sense: the locus of perception and of love, hate, fear, hope, longing, confusion, and other inward states; in reality, it is the human nafs as moved by its powers and emotions. Because God created the human being and every part, faculty, capacity, and action belonging to him, He comprehends and truly possesses them. He stands between the person and his heart, hearing, sight, body, self, and all that pertains to him, granting or withholding their capacities as He wills. The same ontological divine ownership extends to every creature and its essence, powers, effects, and acts.

God is thus nearer to a person than anything attached to him, including his own heart, and has true dominion over its potentialities. The final gathering discloses this dominion: all apparent ownership and authority disappear, and God alone is manifest as the true King. The clause about God’s intervention consequently explains why the call that grants life must be answered.

The true call is tawḥīd. Since God is clearer and nearer to the human being than the heart through which he perceives, no one has an excuse to reject the call through uncertainty about its truth, confusion among madhāhib, or doubts and devilish suggestions in the heart. The human being knows the one Lord before knowing his own heart or other things known through it; the heart may waver about other matters, but it does not genuinely mistake the single Lord of all things.

One must answer this call inwardly as well as verbally, rather than concealing in the heart what contradicts the tongue, for that is hypocrisy and God knows what the heart contains. At the Resurrection He will disclose deeds and inward thoughts. Nor should anyone imagine himself independent master of his heart: faith and doubt, hope and fear, tranquillity and agitation first fall under God’s unrestricted direction and decree. A person who finds faith or reverence within must not feel secure from God’s stratagem; he should believe and resolve upon good in fear that God may turn his heart from happiness to misery. Conversely, one whose heart resists truth or righteous action must hasten to respond to God and His Messenger, without surrendering to despair, because God can rectify and redirect the heart through His succor and mercy.

Thus the verse removes the excuses of rejectors and polytheists, exposes hypocrisy, and teaches believers that they do not independently possess their hearts. It guards those who find faith from self-deception and those who lack spiritual resolve from despair. Al-Mizan judges narrower interpretations inadequate: that the verse is only a severe warning based on God’s nearness, only an assertion that no deeds or words are hidden from Him, only a warning to obey before death prevents repentance, or only a reference to God’s shifting hearts away from fear in battle. A Shiʿi narration likewise gives a particular application: God prevents a person from taking truth for falsehood or falsehood for truth.
verses.25:
Al-Mizan holds that the verse warns all believers, not rejectors, against a fitnah originating among wrongdoers within their own community. Whether read with the common lā tuṣībanna or the reported recitation la-tuṣībanna, the warning shows that the wrongdoing of one sector can bring consequences upon all. The warning that Allah is severe in retribution is unrestricted and cannot be confined to worldly afflictions such as violence, corruption, insecurity, or civil unrest.

The whole Muslim society must therefore prevent and extinguish such fitnah by commanding good and forbidding evil. The warning particularly concerns factionalism and partisanship that divide the community, undermine the word of truth and the upright religion, and allow a group to depart knowingly from truth into oppression. It is not a statement about every individual wrong, but about wrongdoing that spreads from a group through society—such as rebellion against the true Islamic government or concerted destruction of the Qur’an’s and Sunnah’s clear provisions. Its consequences include communal degradation, impoverishment, conflict, captivity, plunder, violated honor, abandonment of the Book, and neglect of the Sunnah; all bear responsibility before God. Since the ummah was warned, its neglect leaves it unable to escape divine punishment.

Majmaʿ al-Bayān reports that Imām al-Sajjād, Imām al-Bāqir, Zayd ibn Thābit, Rabīʿ ibn Anas, and Abū al-ʿĀliyah recited la-tuṣībanna, with la- as an oath and -anna as emphasis: believers are to fear a sedition that will indeed strike the wrongdoers among them exclusively. In this reading, khāṣṣatan qualifies the fitnah. The common reading lā tuṣībanna means that the fitnah may not strike only the unjust; lā is negation, not part of a second command, and the clause continues the warning, like the construction, “Enter your houses, so that Solomon will not smash you.”

Some grammarians instead construe the common reading as an imperative response—“do not let it strike you”—while others call lā superfluous or derive the form from an expanded la-tuṣībanna. Al-Mizan regards the latter two explanations as unlikely and unfitting for God’s speech; in effect they yield the meaning of the alternative reading.

The verse addresses the believing community at large and is reinforced by the preceding summons to the life-giving divine call, which includes unity, establishing religion, and avoiding division. Though contextualized, its import is broader. The commentary maintains that the civil strife that later shattered Muslim unity exemplified the warning, and rejects the attempt to limit the verse’s punishment to this world alone.
verses.26:
Al-Mizan explains mustaḍʿafūn as being treated lightly or deemed weak, yatakhaṭṭafakum as being snatched away, fa-āwākum as being granted a shelter or haven, and ayyadakum as being strengthened.

The verse recalls the Muslims’ condition before the migration: confined in Mecca, few and weak, and fearing seizure by Arab polytheists and the champions of Quraysh. God sheltered them in Medina, strengthened them through His aid at Badr, and supplied them with wholesome things, including spoils.

Though the immediate reference is particularly to the Emigrants, the address includes both Emigrants and Helpers as one community united in faith. Set amid the account of Badr, the verse in itself addresses all Muslims: later Muslims inherited the early community’s victory, shelter in Medina, increase through the Anṣār, divine aid at Badr and elsewhere, and goodly provision, all requiring gratitude.
verses.27:
Al-Mizan explains khiyānah as the opposite of amānah: secretly violating a right or going against a pact or trust. Though khiyānah and nifāq may overlap, khiyānah is especially used for contracts and property, while nifāq concerns religious matters.

The commentary prefers reading “nor knowingly betray your own trusts” as dependent on an implied an: the whole expression forms one prohibition against betraying God and the Messenger by betraying the believers’ own trusts. “Knowingly” means knowing that the act itself is betrayal, not merely knowing its evil consequences or its prohibition. It serves to awaken fiṭrah and rational judgment: one who recognizes that the harm of betrayal returns to himself and his fellow believers should not betray himself. It is not stated merely as a precondition of religious responsibility.

God’s trusts among people include sharīʿah rulings and the Messenger’s beauteous conduct (sīrah); people also hold one another’s wealth and secrets in trust. Other trusts belong jointly to God, the Messenger, and the faithful, including matters that God enjoins, the Messenger administers, and society depends upon—such as political secrets and military plans. Publicizing them unsettles religion, weakens Islamic government, violates the right of God and His Messenger, and harms the believers. Such treachery therefore betrays all three.

The connection with the warning that possessions and children are a test indicates that some Muslims disclosed the Prophet’s secrets to polytheists in hopes of placating them, perhaps out of fear for wealth and children left in Mecca after migration. A report concerning the occasion of revelation supports this: when Gabriel informed the Prophet that Abū Sufyān had departed Mecca with great wealth and instructed him to pursue the matter secretly, someone wrote to Abū Sufyān warning him, whereupon the verse was revealed.

verses.29:
Al-Mizan explains furqān as that by which one thing is distinguished from another. Because it follows taqwā and occurs after commands and prohibitions involving good and evil, it denotes a comprehensive discernment between truth and falsehood: faith and rejection, guidance and misguidance, obedience and disobedience, and whatever pleases or displeases God. The view that it distinguishes right from wrong is included within this wider meaning.

The verse summarizes the preceding injunctions. Whoever reveres God will not be confused about what pleases or displeases Him in these matters; God will also absolve that person’s wrongs and forgive him. This discernment, forgiveness, and absolution are fruits of God’s tremendous bounty.
verses.30:
Al-Mizan reads verses (8:30)–40 as continuing the earlier account of God’s favors and assistance to the believers, except for (8:32)–33, which it judges to be separate from the surrounding Quraysh-centered passage.

In (8:30), makr is diverting someone from his aim by trickery; it may be good, as when attributed to God, or evil, as in an evil plot that returns upon its makers. God’s plot may include giving a person respite and worldly abundance while he remains unaware and deluded. Ithbāt means confinement or imprisonment. The verse recalls the Quraysh’s attempt to extinguish the Prophet’s call by choosing among imprisonment, assassination, and expulsion, while God countered their plot. Their hesitation among these alternatives shows that they had taken counsel, supporting the reports of their conspiracy at Dār al-Nadwah.

In (8:31), asāṭīr means fabricated tales. The faithless claim to have heard the Qur’an and to be able, if they wished, to produce something similar. The use of mithla hādhā, rather than forms that would refer straightforwardly to the signs, conveys their mockery of the divine signs and of the messenger’s position. Though the recited verses plainly establish their divine source and God’s will of the true religion, the opponents disparage them as old fables and profess disinterest in them.

The request in (8:32) to rain stones from the sky calls for a heavenly, annihilating sign. Stones are singled out because they inflict both bodily pain and humiliation, while the indefinite “painful punishment” includes every other form of punishment. The wording, “if this be the truth from You,” presupposes an assertion that this is the exclusive truth from God: it addresses one who acknowledges that God has a true religion and revelation, yet denies that what the Prophet brought is from Him. It therefore affirms both the Prophet’s divinely revealed religion and the exclusive divine origin of what he brought. Al-Mizan considers it likely that these words express a collective position rather than a literal saying of a pagan; they more suitably resemble the words of an apostate or a person from the People of the Book.

The initial possible reading of (8:33) is that the Prophet’s presence in Mecca prevented a heavenly annihilating punishment of the Quraysh before the migration, not punishment through battle or captivity. Yet the commentary finds serious difficulties in taking (8:32)–33 as concerning the Meccan polytheists. If the verse instead protects all Arabs or the whole ummah while the Prophet lives and while they seek forgiveness, it cannot apply to reported speakers such as Abū Jahl or al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥarith ibn Kaladah, who were punished at Badr. It would also sever the reply from the preceding challenge. Reports connecting (8:32) with One demanding, demanded the chastisement which must befall the faithless; there is none to avert it (70:2) add to the difficulty.

Al-Mizan rejects the claim that the Prophet’s being a mercy to the worlds precludes punishment. Mercy requires giving each their due, including calling tyrants to account; God’s all-encompassing mercy did not prevent wrath from reaching earlier peoples. Nor does describing Badr as punishment conflict with And We have only sent you as a mercy to the worlds (21:107). The phrase “while they are seeking forgiveness” overtly promises that punishment will not descend so long as they continually seek forgiveness. But stubborn Meccan idolaters were not such people. Reports that they later said, “Your pardon, O God!” are not established, and forgiveness-seeking by associationists, especially their leaders, cannot nullify their defiant challenge or remove the basis for condemning them.

Nor can the issue be resolved by identifying the promised absence of punishment with an absence of battle, since (8:34)–35 explicitly ask why they should not be punished for barring people from the Sacred Mosque and command them to taste punishment. The proposal that the first half of (8:33) was revealed before the migration and the second afterward also fails: believers seeking forgiveness were present in Mecca before the migration, and the Prophet remained among people afterward. Likewise, interpreting both clauses as guarantees that the ummah will not be obliterated—first because of the Prophet’s presence, then because of its repentance—conflicts with the threat in (8:34).

Thus (8:32)–33 were not revealed with the surrounding discussion of the Quraysh. More likely, their dialogue concerns the People of the Book or persons who accepted Islam and then recanted. Narrations naming al-Ḥārith ibn al-Nuʿmān al-Fihrī support this reading. The verses then mean that, unlike earlier nations, the Muslim ummah will not be exterminated by heavenly punishment while the Prophet is alive among them, or after him while they seek forgiveness. Yet they also portend a future chastisement: eventually the ummah will cease seeking forgiveness and the faithful will no longer remain among it.

Verse (8:34) is an astonished, disavowing question: why should God not punish people who bar believers from the Sacred Mosque when they are not its guardians? The House was founded on reverence for God, so none may exercise authority over it unless they are reverent. “Only the reverent may be its guardians” is an explanatory assertion carrying an implied command, not a conditional authorization of guardianship. Here punishment may mean killing or more generally what follows in the context.

Majmaʿ al-Bayān proposes three reconciliations between this threat and the earlier negation of punishment: the first punishment is annihilation whereas the second is killing, captivity, or the like; the latter punishment is in the hereafter; or immunity lasts as long as they seek forgiveness and repent. Al-Mizan replies that all three depend on wrongly linking (8:34) to the preceding separate verses. Moreover, the earlier context is too severe to support a contrast between kinds of punishment, the context of (8:34)–35 is not about the hereafter, and the third proposal conflicts with the overt requirement of continual repentance.

In (8:35), mukāʾan is whistling and taṣdiyatan is clapping. “Their prayer” refers to the Qurayshi polytheists who barred others from the Sacred House. The command, “So taste the punishment,” announces impending punishment, and the shift from third person to direct address intensifies the threat. The verse is an adverbial continuation of (8:34): they bar God’s faithful servants from the House while their own worship there is mere clapping and whistling. From these verses Al-Mizan infers that leaving the Sacred House empty through barring people from it brings divine punishment; it cites ʿAlī’s testament: “By God, by God, [look after] the House of your Lord. If it is abandoned, you shall not be looked to.”

Verse (8:36) describes the divinely governed failure of those who spend wealth to obstruct God’s way. Disbelief drives them to oppose the divine call, oppress others, and waste their wealth on corrupt aims; they will regret, be overcome, and gain no benefit. Their worldly gathering to promote evil and fight God and His Messenger becomes their gathering into hell. As a Qur’anic prophecy revealed after Badr, the spending and regret apparently refer to Uḥud or another encounter, their defeat to the conquest of Mecca, and their gathering in hell to those who never embrace Islam.

Verse (8:37) explains this outcome through the universal divine sunnah: God separates khabīth, the impure, from ṭayyib, the good, placing each with its own kind. The wicked are piled together and cast into hell, while the righteous reach the Garden. The faithless’ exhausted wealth, efforts, and deeds are therefore futile because creation’s order distinguishes evil from good. This resembles the parable in which foam passes away while what benefits people remains, and shows the universal law that every branch springs from its root.

In (8:38), yantahū means ceasing what is forbidden, mā qad salafa what has passed, and sunnah a way or established course. The Prophet is told to offer both hope and warning: if the faithless stop fighting and sedition, God forgives their former persecution of believers; if they return to it, they should fear the fate of earlier peoples, who were destroyed and whose efforts came to nothing.

Verses (8:39-40) set out the believers’ corresponding duty. Fitnah here is the painful persecution, fighting, insecurity, and violation of treaties by which the Quraysh seized, tortured, and sought to force believers out of Islam, including conduct that continued in Mecca after the migration. Fighting is commanded until such assaults cease, their disbelief no longer deludes them into attacking the faithful, and religion is wholly for God, with no call opposed to Him. If they stop fighting, God sees their deeds and will judge them accordingly; if they resume fighting and strife, the believers must fight, trusting God as the best guardian and helper.

“Religion is entirely for Allah” does not conflict with the People of the Book maintaining their faith under Muslim dhimmah and paying jizyah; hence this verse is not abrogated by until they pay the jizyah by hand while they are subjugated (9:29). Some narrations count “the most superb guardian” and “the most superb helper” among God’s beautiful Names, where “name” denotes what indicates the divine essence through a particular quality rather than an ordinary grammatical noun.
verses.31:
Al-Mizan explains that asāṭīr in (8:31) means fabricated tales. The Qurayshi faithless say, “We have heard,” and claim that, if they wished, they could produce something similar. Their use of mithla hādhā rather than forms referring straightforwardly to the signs signals mockery of both God’s signs and the messenger’s office. Although the Qur’anic verses plainly establish their divine source and God’s will of the true religion, these opponents belittle them as old fables and profess to understand them while rejecting them.

In (8:32), asking God to rain stones from the sky requests a heavenly, annihilating sign. Stones are specified because they bring bodily pain and humiliating abasement, while the indefinite “painful punishment” encompasses other forms of punishment. The words “if this be the truth from You” imply that the Prophet had declared this to be the exclusive truth from God. They address one who recognizes that a true religion and divine message can come from God but denies that what the Prophet brought is from Him; the statement therefore affirms both revealed religion and the divine origin of the Prophet’s message. Al-Mizan considers it more likely that the statement represents a shared position than an actual saying of a pagan, and that it is more fittingly attributed to an apostate or to someone from the People of the Book.

One possible reading of (8:33) is that the Prophet’s presence in Mecca prevented heavenly annihilation from overtaking the Quraysh before the migration; such punishment differs from battle or captivity inflicted through the Prophet’s hand. But Al-Mizan finds this reading, and alternatives that make the verse concern all Arabs or the whole ummah, deeply problematic. If the protection covers the ummah while the Prophet lives and while people seek forgiveness, it does not include reported speakers of (8:32) such as Abū Jahl or al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥarith ibn Kaladah, who were punished at Badr. The reply would then have no connection to the challenge it follows. The reported connection of (8:32) with One demanding, demanded the chastisement which must befall the faithless; there is none to avert it (70:2) further complicates the usual sequencing.

The commentary rejects the claim that the Prophet’s status as a mercy to the worlds rules out punishment. Mercy requires giving all people their due, including holding tyrants accountable; God’s mercy extending to all things did not prevent wrath from reaching ancient peoples. Nor is punishment at Badr inconsistent with And We have only sent you as a mercy to the worlds (21:107). The second clause of (8:33) overtly means that God will not punish them so long as they continually seek forgiveness. Yet the stubborn Meccan polytheists were not going to seek forgiveness for their crimes. Reports that they regretted their statement and said, “Your pardon, O God!” are not established; moreover, the forgiveness-seeking of associationists, particularly their leaders, cannot erase their defiance or deprive the verses of their condemning force.

The next verses make it untenable to say that (8:32)–33 simply suspend punishment for the Quraysh. Verse (8:34) asks why God should not punish people who bar others from the Sacred Mosque, and (8:35) commands them to taste punishment. If (8:32) refers to heavenly punishment for Quraysh idolaters, that does not cohere with the later references to punishment through battle. If it means that they will not face battle, the contradiction is still more evident. Dividing (8:33) into a pre-migration clause and a post-migration clause also fails, since believers seeking forgiveness were present in Mecca before the migration and the Prophet remained among people afterward.

Al-Mizan consequently concludes that (8:32)–33 neither belong to the preceding nor the following Quraysh passage and were not revealed with it. More likely, the dialogue concerns the People of the Book or persons who accepted Islam and then recanted. Narrations identifying the speaker as al-Ḥārith ibn al-Nuʿmān al-Fihrī reinforce this. Under this reading, the verses promise that, unlike earlier nations, the Muslim ummah will not be exterminated by punishment from heaven while the Prophet lives among it, or after him while it seeks forgiveness. At the same time, they foretell that the ummah will eventually abandon forgiveness and the faithful will no longer remain among it, after which punishment will descend.

If the protection covers the ummah while the Prophet lives and while people seek forgiveness, it does not include reported speakers of (8:32) such as Abū Jahl or al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥarith ibn Kaladah, who were punished at Badr. The reply would then have no connection to the challenge it follows. The reported connection of (8:32) with One demanding, demanded the chastisement which must befall the faithless; there is none to avert it (70:2) further complicates the usual sequencing.

Mercy requires giving all people their due, including holding tyrants accountable; God’s mercy extending to all things did not prevent wrath from reaching ancient peoples. If it means that they will not face battle, the contradiction is still more evident. Al-Mizan explains that asāṭīr in (8:31) means fabricated tales. The Qurayshi faithless say, “We have heard,” and claim that, if they wished, they could produce something similar. Their use of mithla hādhā rather than forms referring straightforwardly to the signs signals mockery of both God’s signs and the messenger’s office. Although the Qur’anic verses plainly establish their divine source and God’s will of the true religion, these opponents belittle them as old fables and profess to understand them while rejecting them.

In (8:32), asking God to rain stones from the sky requests a heavenly, annihilating sign. Stones are specified because they bring bodily pain and humiliating abasement, while the indefinite “painful punishment” encompasses other forms of punishment. The words “if this be the truth from You” imply that the Prophet had declared this to be the exclusive truth from God. They address one who recognizes that a true religion and divine message can come from God but denies that what the Prophet brought is from Him; the statement therefore affirms both revealed religion and the divine origin of the Prophet’s message. verses.34:
Al-Mizan takes (8:34) as an astonished, disavowing question: why should God not punish people who bar believers from the Sacred Mosque even though they are not its guardians? The clauses describe them as barring others and lacking guardianship. Since the House was founded upon reverence for God, no one may exercise authority over it, admitting or excluding whom he wishes, unless he is reverent. “Only the reverent may be its guardians” is an explanatory assertion with an implied command, not a conditional statement granting guardianship to the reverent. The punishment may mean killing or a broader punishment indicated by the following context.

Majmaʿ al-Bayān offers three ways to reconcile this threat with the earlier denial of punishment: the first punishment is annihilation and the second killing, captivity, or similar treatment; the latter is punishment in the hereafter; or immunity lasts only while they seek forgiveness and turn to God. Al-Mizan rejects these answers because they assume that this verse is connected to the preceding verses, whereas it has argued that it is not. Further, the earlier context is too severe to permit a contrast merely between two kinds of punishment; (8:34)–35 concern worldly punishment, not the hereafter; and the last proposal conflicts with the overt meaning that forgiveness must be continual.
verses.35:
Al-Mizan explains mukāʾan as whistling and taṣdiyatan as clapping. “Their prayer” concerns the Qurayshi polytheists who barred people from the Sacred House. The command, “So taste the punishment for what you used to deny,” announces their impending punishment; its shift from third-person description to direct plural address intensifies the threat.

The verse is an adverbial continuation of the preceding verse: they bar God’s faithful servants from the Sacred House while their own worship there is mere play in whistling and clapping. From these two verses, the commentary infers that leaving the Sacred House empty by barring people from it brings divine punishment. It cites ʿAlī’s testament: “By God, by God, [look after] the House of your Lord. If it is abandoned, you shall not be looked to.”
verses.36:
Al-Mizan explains that those who reject faith spend their wealth trying to extinguish God’s call and obstruct His way, but their efforts necessarily fail: they waste their wealth, regret it, are overcome, and are gathered into hell. Disbelief impels them toward opposition, oppression, and wickedness, none of which can yield success or salvation under God’s cause-and-effect sunnah. Their worldly assembly to promote evil and fight God and His Messenger becomes, on the Day of Resurrection, their assembly in hell.

The verse is also a Qur’anic prophecy. Revealed after Badr, it apparently points to spending and regret at Uḥud or another encounter, defeat at the conquest of Mecca, and gathering in hell for those who never embrace Islam.
verses.37:
Al-Mizan explains yumayyizu as separating a thing from its opposite and joining it to its own kind; khabīth is the opposite of ṭayyib, and fa-yarkumahu means piling things atop one another. The verse explains why the faithless’ efforts to extinguish God’s light are futile: they exhaust wealth and effort in vain, becoming regretful and defeated.

Their fate follows the universal divine sunnah operating throughout creation: God separates evil from good and wicked people from righteous ones, then heaps the wicked together and casts them into hell, while the good reach the Garden. This resembles the parable in which worthless foam passes away and what benefits people remains. It expresses the universal law that every branch springs from its root.
verses.38: Al-Mizan explains yantahū as stopping an act because it is forbidden, mā qad salafa as what has passed, and sunnah as an established way. The Prophet is commanded to give the faithless both hope and warning: if they desist from fighting and sedition, God will forgive their former persecution and torment of the believers; if they return to their forbidden conduct, they must beware the fate of earlier peoples, who were utterly destroyed and whose efforts were laid waste.
verses.39:
Al-Mizan presents (8:39-40) as the believers’ duty corresponding to the warning addressed to the faithless. The believers must continue striving to establish the religion and a sound environment for them, fighting until fitnah ceases. Here fitnah is the painful persecution, fighting, insecurity, and violation of treaties by which the Quraysh seized believers, tortured them, and tried to force them from Islam; this continued in Mecca for a time after the migration.

Thus, “Fight them until there is no more strife” figuratively commands weakening them until their disbelief no longer moves them to assault the faithful, and until religion is wholly for God with no call opposed to Him. If they cease fighting, God sees their deeds and will judge them accordingly. If they return to fighting and strife, the believers must also resume fighting, confident that God is their guardian and helper.

“Religion is entirely for Allah” does not conflict with the People of the Book continuing in their faith under Muslim dhimmah and paying jizyah. Therefore, the verse is not abrogated by until they pay the jizyah by hand while they are subjugated (9:29). According to some narrations, “the most superb guardian” and “the most superb helper” are among God’s beautiful Names, where “name” does not mean an ordinary grammatical noun but what denotes the divine essence through a particular quality.

verses.41:
Al-Mizan explains that ghunm and ghanīmah denote gain or profit, whether obtained through trade, work, or battle, though the immediate setting of the verse is war-spoils. Dhū al-qurbā means a relative and here denotes the Prophet’s kinsfolk, or particular members of his family, as indubitable narrations establish; yatīm is a human child who loses his father while young.

The grammatical alternatives for fa-anna lillāhi wa lil-rasūli—whether an implied preposition is understood, a predicate is omitted, or the fāʾ introduces a conditional consequence—ultimately yield the same sense: whatever is acquired, one fifth is due to Allah, the Messenger, and the designated recipients. Allah’s name is placed first in honour. “If you believe in Allah” conditions compliance with this command and cannot plausibly be attached to the more distant preceding verse.

The commentary holds that “what We revealed to Our servant” most readily refers to the Qur’an, rather than to the angels sent at Badr. Had angels been intended, the wording would have referred to their being sent down and would have addressed the believers as well as the Prophet. The shift from third person to first person in “what We revealed to Our servant” manifests God’s grace in drawing His Messenger near. In light of the opening of the sūrah, the revelation at Badr concerns the spoils: they belong to Allah and the Messenger, though God permitted the believers to consume and expend part of them while commanding them to remit a fifth to those entitled to it. Badr is the day of sorting because God distinguished truth from falsehood by supporting the former and abandoning the latter; His power over all things explains His power to make this distinction.

Al-Mizan takes the verse as an enduring legal injunction, not one confined to battlefield booty. Khums applies to everything properly called ghanam or ghanīmah, including war gains, trade and wages, diving, seafaring, buried treasure, and mining. The named recipients restrict its expenditure to them, and each has an independent share, as appears in the verse on zakāt. This reading follows the apparent wording and is reinforced by Shiʿi narrations, whereas Sunni exegetes differ over the verse’s interpretation.
verses.42:
Al-Mizan explains that ʿudwah is the slope of a wadi, with the believers on the nearer slope and their enemies on the farther one; the rakb is said to be Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb’s trade caravan. “When you were on the canyon-side” is most naturally a further clarification of the day of sorting and of what was revealed to the Prophet, though some take it as explaining God’s power to aid the believers despite their small number; the latter reading is somewhat convoluted.

“Had you made a tryst with each other, you would have broken the tryst” means that the encounter was not arranged through planning, consultation, or ordinary causes. God placed the powerful polytheists on the farther, watered, hard ground and the few believers on the nearer, sandy, dry ground, then brought the two sides face to face with no barrier or escape. The believers’ victory therefore displayed divine care and assistance rather than natural military causes.

God brought about this decreed event so that truth and falsity would be made plainly evident: He aided the believers and forsook the polytheists. Thus “perishing” and “living” primarily concern misguidance and guidance, each occurring upon clear proof. Allah’s being Hearing and Knowing indicates that He heard their supplications and knew what was within them. The simultaneous encampment and battle were consequently a divinely decreed sign and conclusive proof, not a prearranged meeting.
verses.43:
Al-Mizan understands the verse as calling the believers to remember how God showed the enemy to the Prophet in a dream as few. Fashal is fearful weakness, tanāzuʿ is disputation, and sallama means that God saved them. By showing the opponents as few, God strengthened the believers’ hearts and gave them ease; had their number been shown as great and the Prophet then told them so, they would have recoiled in fear and disputed whether to advance.

The dream was glad tidings of God’s promise regarding one of the two sides. The Prophet conveyed it to the believers, who consequently resolved to march forth. God saved them from fear and disagreement because He knows what lies within hearts and knows what repairs and strengthens them amid wavering between confidence and doubt.
verses.44: Al-Mizan holds that the verse describes the opening of the encounter at Badr: God made each side appear few to the other so that His decreed matter would be brought about. There is no contradiction with the statement that the unbelievers later saw the believers as twice their own number (3:13). At first, while they were at the wadi, the polytheists saw the believers as few and therefore underestimated them and hastened down to fight. Once they had descended, spread out, and mingled with the believers, the latter appeared numerous to them; their resolve collapsed, their hearts fled, and they were defeated. Thus Sūrah al-Anfāl concerns the beginning of the battle, while Sūrah Āl-i ʿImrān concerns its later stage.
verses.45:
Al-Mizan treats these verses as a comprehensive regulation for believers in battle. They must stand firm before the enemy and not flee. This steadfastness is broader than ṣabr: patience is a particular steadfastness in which the heart does not weaken, fear, or become troubled before what it dislikes, and the body does not become idle, inattentive, or leave its proper place.

They must remember Allah much, inwardly and verbally. In the context of battle, this means recalling that death and life are in God’s hand, that He can aid them, that He is their guardian, and that He has promised assistance to those who aid Him. Fighting then has two good outcomes: victory, by which Islam is raised and its religious fruits may flourish, or martyrdom, by which one approaches God’s mercy, generosity, and awliyāʾ. “Much” remembrance renews God-consciousness whenever attachment to worldly adornment or Satanic suggestion arises.

They must obey the commands and prohibitions God has issued through the Messenger concerning warfare and the defence of the community and Islam. They must not quarrel, because disagreement weakens resolve, unity, strength, rule, and victory; rīḥ accordingly signifies might, rule, or victory. They must patiently endure the hardships and threats of war, while remembering and obeying God, so that events do not shake them, obedience does not become burdensome, sin does not tempt them, and vainglory does not mislead them. God’s being with the patient means that patience is the strongest support in distress, enabling calm and sound thought when hardship scatters the mind.

The believers must also not imitate the Qurayshī faithless, who went forth in exultation, hypocrisy, and display, while barring others from God’s way. Baṭar is the levity and bewilderment born from abusing prosperity, and riʾāʾ is presenting oneself as other than one is. To bar people from God’s path is to induce abandonment of God-consciousness and obedience, indulgence in sin, and the consequent frustration of deeds and extinguishing of faith’s light. Allah comprehends their deeds: they remain within His authority and decree and cannot thwart Him. The six requirements—firmness, abundant remembrance, obedience to Allah and His Messenger, avoidance of quarrelling, avoidance of boastful display, and not obstructing God’s way—together leave nothing essential out of the conduct of war. The victories and defeats in the Prophet’s battles depended on observing or neglecting this divine ordinance.

verses.48:
Al-Mizan explains Satan’s making deeds seem fair as implanting in hearts the sense that evil acts are good and delightful, stirring the relevant faculties and emotions until their consequences are no longer considered. The “deeds” may mean the outcomes and preparations of the polytheists’ expedition—mustering men, weapons, and other means and arranging the army—or their actual wrongdoing, temptation, oppression, and persistence in opposing God and His Messenger. Satan’s assurance that none could overcome them, followed by his promise of protection, completed this deception. His claim to be their jār invokes the pre-Islamic custom by which a neighbour or tribal associate gave protection and aid.

When the forces met, Satan recoiled and fled. “I see what you see not” may refer to angels descending to aid the believers, and his fear of Allah’s severe retribution explains his abandonment of the polytheists. Thus he had urged them inwardly to fight the believers and rejoice in their preparations; but when divine aid descended, their imagined courage and victory became fear, despair, and loss.

The commentary also considers that Satan appeared in a human form perceptible to them, tempted them into battle, and then fled upon seeing the divine aid. Shiʿi and Sunni narrations report that he manifested as Surāqah ibn Mālik ibn Jushʿum al-Kinānī, also called al-Mudlijī, a chief of Kinānah, encouraged the polytheists, bore their banner until the forces met, and then escaped. Some exegetes reject this view and weaken its narrations in favour of an inward, metaphorical interpretation. Al-Mizan says that the reports are not mutawātir and lack proofs that would make their reliability wholly certain, but their central claim is rationally possible and does not conflict with authenticated accounts: nothing prevents Satan from taking human form and misleading the polytheists until they are destroyed or until he sees divine punishment. The context, especially “while I am your defender,” his turning back when the hosts meet, and “I see what you see not,” more readily fits the second interpretation than a merely metaphorical seeing.
verses.49:
Al-Mizan explains the hypocrites as people who professed faith while concealing unbelief, and the sick-hearted as people of weak faith who retained doubts. They mocked the believers as people deceived by religion for advancing with a small, poorly equipped force against the Quraysh’s numbers, equipment, and strength.

The reply, “But whoever trusts in Allah—Allah is Mighty, Wise,” shows that the mockers themselves were deceived. The believers entrust their affairs to God and return matters to Him despite the presence of material causes; through this reliance they attach themselves to His power. God suffices one who entrusts a matter to Him, for He is Mighty in aiding those who seek His aid and Wise in disposing of affairs without error.

The verse indicates that hypocrites and weak believers were present when the forces met at Badr. Since hypocrites outwardly accepted Islam while inwardly rejecting it, they must have been among the Muslims, whereas those of weak faith and doubt could have been on either side. It is said that some had accepted Islam in Mecca but were confined by their fathers and forced to march with the Quraysh; seeing the Muslims’ small and unprepared force, they declared that religion had deceived them. The severe occasion showed that only those whose hearts were true in faith and who relied on non-material aid could stand firm.
verses.50:
Al-Mizan explains yatawaffā as taking something fully, a term commonly used in the Qur’an for taking the soul at death. The attribution of this act here to angels does not conflict with verses attributing it to the Angel of Death or to Allah: the Angel of Death has assisting angels under his command, and he himself acts by God’s command. Thus all three attributions are valid.

The angels’ smiting faces and backs most apparently means striking the front and rear of the disbelievers’ bodies, indicating that they are surrounded and struck from every side. Some exegetes instead understand the expression as a figurative description of complete humiliation. The angels tell them to taste the burning punishment, namely the Fire. Whether the statement about what their hands have wrought continues the angels’ speech or comments on the whole event, it establishes that the striking and punishment result from their own deeds.

Allah never wrongs any of His servants: He remains on the straight path and does not contradict His acts. Were He to wrong even one servant, He would be a ẓallām toward all His servants. From the context, the disbelievers being smitten and tormented are the Qurayshī polytheists killed at Badr.
