verses.52: Al-Mizan explains daʾb and daydan as a persistent habit or a path one follows. The unbelief of those addressed resembles the habitual unbelief of Pharaoh’s people and the earlier destroyed nations: they rejected God’s signs, sinned, and were therefore seized for their faults. Allah is strong and not unable to seize them; when He does seize them, His retribution is severe.
verses.53:
Al-Mizan presents the verse as a universal divine law: blessings remain with a people so long as they do not change themselves. Blessings flow in accordance with a people’s readiness to receive them; only when they alter this capacity and become fit for punishment do blessings change into retribution. Applied here, the law explains the chastisement of the Qurayshī polytheists for their crimes.

The more general principle, “Allah does not change what is with a people until they change what is inside them selves (13:11),” includes both the transformation of blessing into punishment and punishment into blessing, whereas this verse more specifically concerns blessing becoming retribution. “Allah is Hearing, Knowing” supplies a second explanation: God may be understood as hearing people’s pleas and knowing their needs, thus answering them and chastising their enemies; or as hearing their words and knowing their deeds, thus chastising them for these. Both meanings may be combined.
verses.54:
Al-Mizan explains that this verse echoes 8:52 to connect two analogous cases. Verse 8:52 reflects upon punishment for what people’s hands have wrought and God’s lack of injustice, while (8:54) reflects upon the law that God does not withdraw a blessing until people change themselves. The variation from “Allah destroyed them” to “We destroyed them” may suit the latter context: blessings emanate from God to His servants, while the people themselves spoil them by departing from the straight path.

The shift from kafarū bi-āyāt Allāh in 8:52 to kadhdhabū bi-āyāt-i rabbihim, and from “Allah” to the first-person plural “We,” conveys the gravity of the matter and indicates agents or intermediaries who act by God’s command. The explicit naming of Pharaoh’s people as those drowned avoids uncertainty over whether the drowning concerned them alone or also the earlier peoples. Divine punishment seized the Qurayshī faithless, Pharaoh’s people, and those before them because all were wrongdoers. God subjects people to severe torment or withdraws blessing only when they have become characterized by ẓulm and rejection of His signs; He chastises only those who deserve it.
verses.55:
Al-Mizan explains that calling them “the vilest of beasts before Allah” is an inerrant divine judgment: no good can be hoped for from them, so defence against them is required by every suitable possible means. It introduces the command concerning them in war.

“Those who reject [Him]” and “they will not believe” express cause and effect: their entrenched kufr causes their refusal of faith, rather than mere absence of faith necessarily producing kufr. The verse concerns the particular people in whom rejection has become so fixed in the heart that it cannot be uprooted and faith can never arise. Thus it refers back to the deaf and dumb bereft of understanding in (8:22-23), whom God knows to contain no good.
verses.56: Al-Mizan takes minhum as partitive: this concerns a particular group among the rejectors with whom the Prophet made an agreement, namely the treaty-violators. “Each time” signifies that they repeatedly broke their pact. Their conduct shows that they feared neither God nor the Muslims and were unafraid of violating their agreements.
verses.57:
Al-Mizan explains tathqafannahum as speedily overcoming and coming upon them, and tashrīd as scattering people in panic. The emphatic wording concerns meeting these treaty-breakers in war: they are to be fought and dealt a crushing blow that disperses and intimidates those who come after them, weakening their resolve and united purpose against the faithful and the truth.

“That they might be reminded” expresses the hope that others will take heed of the consequences of breaking treaties, spreading disorder, and departing from the truth. The verse thus indicates fighting and defeating them so as to deter further people like them who would violate agreements and ambush the truth and its followers.
verses.58:
Al-Mizan explains khiyānah here as breaking a ratified treaty or pact, nabdh as casting or throwing back, and sawāʾ as fairness and equal terms. Fear means the appearance of signs of an impending danger.

If a party to a treaty gives cause to fear that it will violate the agreement, the treaty must first be openly thrown back to it: it must be informed that the covenant is abolished, so that both sides stand on equal terms. Attacking before this declaration would itself be treachery, which Allah does not love.

Together with the preceding verse, this establishes that the rightful leader (walī al-amr) may strike harshly those without a treaty and, after notifying them of the treaty’s abolition, those whose treachery is feared. But a party that neither violates its treaty nor gives cause to fear violation must be held to its agreement, as affirmed by: Observe the treaty with them to the end of the term (9:4) and Fulfill your pacts (5:1).
verses.59: Al-Mizan notes the common recitation taḥsabanna, addressed to the Prophet to strengthen and gladden him, alongside the less common yaḥsabanna. Sabaq means to outstrip or get ahead, and iʿjāz means rendering incapable. The verse means that the Prophet must not suppose the rejectors can outpace God or escape His reach: they cannot thwart or incapacitate Him, for He has power over all things.
verses.60:
Al-Mizan interprets iʿdād as readying the means needed to attain an aim, and quwwah as everything usable in warfare: mounts, armour, weapons, trained fighters, and military pacts. Ribāṭ al-khayl denotes firmly tethered horses. The verse is therefore a comprehensive command to the faithful to prepare all possible military strength, whether or not an enemy is presently before them.

The commentary holds that conflict among human societies, divided by competing natures and creeds, is unavoidable, and that human defensive capacities show the need to prepare against attack. The Islamic society must accordingly muster forces and defences. Since the revealed fiṭrī religion protects the rights and interests of every class and individual rather than yielding to a tyrant or a bare majority, an enemy threatens every member of society. This accounts, possibly, for the command being addressed to the people: defence is the responsibility of all, even though governments principally assemble armies; individuals can also acquire military knowledge and training.

The known enemies are called Allah’s enemy and the believers’ enemy because that is their reality and because the designation urges action. “Others besides them, whom you do not know” requires vigilance toward hidden enemies, including hypocrites who outwardly display faith, as well as persistent kuffār. The intended frightening is deterrence through a display of force.

Military preparation protects society, lives, women, wealth, and, ultimately, religion itself: it extinguishes corruption that destroys the word of truth and the dīn al-fiṭrah through which God is worshipped and justice established. Expenditure in Allah’s way for this purpose benefits the whole Islamic society and is not lost but repaid to the spender in this world and the hereafter. This includes wealth, status, and even one’s life when given in jihad; martyrdom brings true eternal life, unlike dying for worldly fame or glory. The promise that no one is treated unjustly reassures believers that no right is lost. “Whatever you spend in Allah’s way” is broader than “whatever you spend for good shall be repaid to you” (2:272), because the latter concerns wealth while the former also includes offering one’s life.
verses.61:
Al-Mizan explains janaḥū as inclining and salm or silm as peace. The verse gives one combined command: if the enemy inclines to reconciliation and mutual harmony, the Muslims should likewise incline to it while trusting in Allah. They need not fear that a concealed plot will overcome them, for God hears and knows, is not unaware of events arising through natural causes, and cannot be defeated by deception; He will aid and suffice them.

Trust in Allah does not mean abandoning visible natural causes. It means refusing to rely on them absolutely, since human beings perceive only part of the complete causes, all of which turn upon the divine will. Neglecting natural causes in the name of trust would be ignorance.
verses.62:
Al-Mizan presents this verse as answering the concern that an enemy’s apparent inclination to peace may be deception. The command to accept peace is nevertheless accompanied by trust in Allah: if they intend deceit, Allah suffices the Prophet and the believers. Hidden causes beyond ordinary natural causes support the welfare of one who trusts in God, even when natural causes bring betrayal or fail to secure his right.

“He it is who strengthened you with His help and with the believers” provides the evidence for Allah’s sufficiency: God had already aided the Prophet and the faithful and united their formerly hostile hearts.
verses.63:
Al-Mizan explains allafa as uniting through love and goodwill. God’s uniting of the believers’ hearts demonstrates how He suffices one who trusts in Him: He aided His Prophet through the faithful, reconciling people whose long-standing wars had made them enemies and turning them into brethren. Though presented in the setting of the Helpers, the statement applies to all believers.

The commentary argues that human beings naturally seek what benefits themselves, love acquisition, and hate deprivation. Because they must live socially while differing in capacities, circumstances, possessions, and ambitions, rivalry over wealth, position, and other worldly goods produces miserliness, aggression, hatred, bloodshed, and social upheaval. A society whose end is only worldly material prosperity cannot eradicate this corruption: competition and differences remain. Giving or persuading people to accept their circumstances may ease particular conflicts, but cannot uproot the desire to possess and dominate; some goods, such as supreme rule, cannot be shared. Nor do societies ordinarily pursue another society’s material welfare except where it serves themselves.

God removed this hatred from the Muslim community through knowledge of the divine and the teaching that human life is eternal. True happiness is not material consumption but the enduring life of worship, nearness to God, and His pleasure. A believer uses worldly provision while recognizing its rights, receives what is pleasant as a gift from God, and knows that deprivation has a more lasting recompense with Him. He therefore seeks beneficial knowledge and righteous deeds, knowing that benefit and harm, life and death, riches and poverty are in God’s hands.

This does not abolish natural causes or the human drive to work and earn; these remain connected with attaining wholesome ends. But when Muslims are educated by divine teaching and turn their desire from contested material aims to spiritual provision, in which there is neither competition nor deprivation, enmity and avarice are removed. By God’s blessing they become brethren and attain true victory.
verses.64:
Al-Mizan says that the verse raises the Prophet’s spirits. Allah’s sufficiency means, and God knows best, that He aided the Prophet and his faithful followers; it does not posit two sufficient causes, or a single sufficient cause composed of God and the believers, since this would conflict with Qur’anic tawḥīd. It is also possible that “the faithful who follow you” is conjoined to “suffices.”

The context and external evidence place the verse in the setting of urging believers to fight, where divine sufficiency is most immediately relevant. Some exegetes hold that it was revealed in the desert before Badr and thus is not connected to the verses before or after it.
verses.65:
Al-Mizan explains ḥarriḍ as urging or exhorting. The verse states that twenty patient believers overcome two hundred rejectors, and one hundred believers overcome one thousand, because the latter are a people without understanding. This clause gives the cause of the prescribed ten-to-one strength.

Faith gives believers a distinct, unwavering strength grounded in true understanding: bravery, boldness, rectitude, tranquillity, trust in God, and certainty of one of two good ends—being killed and entering Paradise, or fighting and entering Paradise. The faithless, by contrast, rely on fancies and Satanic delusions and regard death as final extinction. That fear unsettles them in terror and prevents steadfast pursuit of their ends. The defeat of the much larger polytheist force at Badr illustrates the contrast between the believers’ understanding, knowledge, and faith and the faithless people’s ignorance, faithlessness, and futility.
verses.66:
Al-Mizan explains that Allah’s knowledge of weakness among the believers means weakness of faith and spiritual certainty, not lack of numbers or military power. Certainty produces the virtues needed for victory, including bravery, patience, and right judgment. Victory over twice their number is “by the permission of Allah,” which is explained by Allah’s being with the patient: it depends on divine will and on patience.

Together, (8:65) and (8:66) show that victory is affected by the spiritual traits of both sides—understanding or its absence, faith or spiritual weakness, and patience. The first measure depicts a believer’s inner strength as equal to ten faithless people; the second lightens the burden to one against two because, by that later condition, the average believer’s inner strength had diminished by eighty percent.

The commentary relates this decline to a general social pattern. A small community pursuing a material or religious aim is initially pressed by trials, becomes alert and self-sacrificing, and gains strength. Once it achieves security, territory, numbers, and ease, the inner ardour that drove it weakens. As numbers increase, weaker faith, diseased hearts, and hypocrisy also increase, lowering the community’s average spiritual strength. This applies to religious and secular aḥzāb alike. The Prophet’s battles illustrate it: the Muslims prevailed at Badr while few and poorly equipped, whereas later events, especially Ḥunayn, showed that great numbers do not avail a people.

The verse thus indicates that as Islam outwardly gained power during the Prophet’s lifetime, the common Muslims’ faith and noble spiritual qualities fell to a fifth of their earlier level. Verses (8:65-66) nevertheless appear to have been revealed together: although they measure believers at two different times, the second is framed by the first, and their differing rulings do not require separate revelations.

Although phrased declaratively, the two verses function as successive commands. The earlier ruling obliges fighting when believers are at least one to ten, while the later ruling requires it when they are at least one to two; the latter mitigates the former. Patience makes one person equal to two, while understanding makes one person equal to five; one who has both equals ten of his like. Patience is never absent from understanding, though understanding can be absent from patience, and patience is indispensable in combat.
verses.67:
Al-Mizan explains that asr is the apprehension and binding of an enemy fighter, so an asīr is a bound captive; sabī is broader and may include an unbound captive. To subdue (yuthkhina) the land means to overcome it so that religion is firmly established among its people. The image is of religion becoming weighty, solid, and enduring after being vulnerable and evanescent. ʿAraḍ denotes passing things and thus the perishable goods of worldly life. Ḥalāl suggests that prohibition has been untied from a thing, while ṭayyib means fit to be eaten.

The commentary notes that exegetes agree that these verses came after Badr, censuring the fighters and permitting them to use war booty, but differ over whom the reproach addresses because of divergent, even apparently contradictory, narrations. Those reports, even if authentic, display considerable transmission by meaning rather than exact wording. The proposed views include that the rebuke concerns the Prophet and all believers, with various exceptions; the believers but not the Prophet; or those who proposed ransom.

Al-Mizan rejects the claim that they were blamed for taking ransom or booty before divine permission. Ransom was taken after these verses, whereas the fighters had already taken captives when the reproach came. Moreover, the Prophet would not declare something lawful before revelation, nor could God threaten His protected Prophet with punishment for no sin; the threatened chastisement indicates a grave, not a lesser, sin.

Rather, “It is not for a prophet to take captives until he subdues the land” states a divine way followed by earlier prophets. When they defeated enemies before their religion had taken firm root, they killed them in order to deter further threats to God and His Messenger. Captives could be taken only after control of the land and establishment of religion, when they might be ransomed or released graciously. The later command, revealed after Islam was firmly established in the Ḥijaz and Yemen, permits this: “So when you meet in battle those who disbelieve, then smite the necks until when you have overcome them, then make [them] prisoners, and afterwards either set them free as a favor or let them ransom [themselves]… . (47:4)”

The context therefore shows that the reproach concerns taking captives, as confirmed by the threatened doom for “what you took.” They had captured prisoners but had not yet collected ransom. Verse 8:69, introduced as a consequence of what precedes, then permits war gains, including ransom. The fighters had asked to ransom the prisoners and receive the proceeds, just as they had asked for the anfāl; reports even state that nearly 280,000 dirhams of ransom was collected. Thus God first censures their taking of captives and then permits their exchange for ransom.

Al-Mizan maintains that the Prophet is not among those censured: neither the verse nor the narrations says that he advised or approved taking captives. Capturing survivors for enslavement or ransom was a military custom among the Migrants and Helpers. Narrations report that they competed to seize captives and guarded their own prisoners, whereas ʿAlī killed many men without taking captives.

The plural address is to the fighters at Badr, most of whom had proposed this course. Their desire for fleeting worldly goods is contrasted with Allah’s desire for the hereafter: the establishment of religion and battle against the faithless. Allah’s might and wisdom affirm the faultlessness of this divine sunnah. The prior ordinance—that God would not rain down punishment on or annihilate them—is left indefinite in order to intensify the rebuke and prevent the command from being trivialized. The threatened doom again shows the enormity of their act. What they took was the captives, not booty or ransom, since those had not yet been obtained; the latter are now declared lawful and wholesome. “Eat then” permits the use of all wartime acquisition, whether property taken from idolaters or ransom. The closing command to mind Allah and the description of Him as forgiving and merciful may either explain this permission as forgiveness and mercy, or explain the whole preceding matter as a merciful permission rather than punishment.

verses.70: Al-Mizan says that the captives being “in your hands” signifies their complete defeat and the Muslims’ control over them. “If Allah knows any good in your hearts” is a figurative expression for faith, or for following the truth inseparable from faith, since the promised forgiveness cannot accompany polytheism. If faith becomes firmly rooted in their hearts—and God knows best whether it has truly taken root—Allah will give them something better than the ransom taken from them and forgive them, for He is forgiving and merciful.
verses.71: Al-Mizan explains amkana minhum as giving the Prophet power over them. Their intended betrayal was to ransom themselves, form another alliance, and attack him; their earlier betrayal of Allah was their denial, attempt to extinguish God’s light, and plotting. If they believe and faith is firmly established in their hearts, Allah will compensate them with something better than what was taken from them and forgive them. But if they return to their former obduracy and wickedness, Allah, who knows their treachery and is wise, has already given the Prophet power over them and can do so again.
verses.72:
Al-Mizan explains that those who believed, migrated, and strove are the first Migrants before this chapter’s revelation, while those who gave shelter and aid are the Helpers who sheltered the Prophet and the emigrant faithful and aided God and His Messenger. Apart from a few Meccan believers who had not migrated, these two groups then comprised the Muslims.

Their being guardians of each other (awliyāʾ) establishes a comprehensive wilāyah—“alliance,” “guardianship,” or “loyalty”—rather than merely authority in inheritance, mutual-aid, or non-aggression arrangements. Its unconditional wording means that a pledge of security given by one Migrant or Helper to a faithless person bound all Muslims.

The commentary rejects the claim that this concerns the Prophet’s earlier pact of brotherhood between Migrants and Helpers, under which they temporarily inherited from one another; the verse provides no evidence for that reading. Believers who did not migrate were outside the formal protection of the Migrants and Helpers until they migrated, though they must be aided when they seek help for religion, unless this would violate a Muslim treaty with non-believers.
verses.73:
Al-Mizan explains that the faithless protect one another but do not extend that protection to the faithful; consequently, the faithful may not take them as allies. Though phrased declaratively, the verse is legislation and command: loyalty assigned to the faithless entails that their allegiance does not include the faithful.

This division of loyalties prevents chaos and grave corruption. Every society requires alliances, especially the Islamic society, which follows truth and spreads divine justice. Alliance with the faithless (kuffār), enemies of this society, produces intermixing through which their beliefs and customs enter Muslim society, corrupting its clear path to truth by their pursuit of vain desires and servitude to Satan. Events of that time testify to this warning.
verses.74: Al-Mizan explains that believing, migrating, striving in Allah’s way, and giving shelter and aid are the effects of true faith. Whoever manifests them is a true believer and is promised forgiveness and a generous sustenance.
verses.75:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse addresses the first Migrants and Helpers and includes all who later believe, migrate, and strive with them; all are guardians of one another.

“Blood relatives have a greater claim on each other in the Book of Allah” assigns wilāyah among kinsfolk with respect to inheritance, without restricting other forms of mutual guardianship to kin. The verse abrogates the earlier decree under which Migrants and Helpers joined in brotherhood inherited from one another. It establishes inheritance by blood relationship, whether the relative is a specified inheritor within the sahm, a paternal relative (ʿaṣabah), or otherwise; its ruling is apparently absolute.
